sections.h2: What the Maine homestead exemption takes off
sections.html:
The Maine homestead exemption lowers the taxable value of your permanent home by up to $25,000. The amount is adjusted by your town's certified ratio, so a town with an 80% ratio gives an exemption of $20,000. It cannot exceed the value of the homestead itself.

Under 36 M.R.S. §683 the $25,000 has two pieces: $10,000 of just value in the base subsection, plus an additional $15,000 for tax years that began on or after April 1, 2020. It sits on top of other exemptions a homeowner may already hold, such as those in sections 653 and 654-A. It is not a credit on the bill. It shrinks the value the town multiplies by its tax rate.

The exemption is tied to a person who lives in the house, not to the house itself. When ownership or residence changes, the break stops and the next owner has to qualify separately.

You qualify if you are a permanent Maine resident, the home is your permanent residence, and you have owned a home in Maine for the twelve months before you apply.

  • Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not count. You can have only one permanent residence at a time.
  • The home must be residential property assessed as real property. A mobile home on a rented lot may qualify.
  • Permanent residence is presumed to continue until circumstances show otherwise. The test is whether you intend to return when you are away.
  • There is no income limit, but renters do not qualify.
  • With several owners, one signature is enough on the application. The exemption can be divided among co-owners who live there in proportion to their interests.

A person who loses a homestead to tax lien foreclosure and later gets it back from the municipality is treated as having owned it the whole time. The town's brief ownership does not disqualify them.

File a written application with your municipal assessor on or before April 1. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment, so a late application costs a full tax year of savings.

Most towns hand out the form, and Maine Revenue Services posts it on its property tax forms page. For an owner-occupied house the town where the property sits and the town where you live are the same, so call the assessor if yours is not.

You do not need to renew every year. The exemption stays in place as long as ownership and residency stay the same. If an assessor denies the application, the notice must give reasons, and you can appeal in writing to the local Board of Assessment Review or the county commissioners. Denials of homestead, veteran and blind exemptions can also go through the abatement process.

The old section 683 discontinues its exemptions for property tax years beginning on or after April 1, 2027, and a new section, 36 M.R.S. §683-A, takes over from that date. The base homestead exemption stays at $25,000 of just value, and veteran and blind exemptions move into the same statute.

ExemptionAmount from April 1, 2027
Base homestead exemption (§683-A)Up to $25,000 of just value
Veteran, age 62 or olderUp to $6,000
Veteran with 100% service-connected ratingUp to $50,000
Legally blind permanent residentUp to $5,000

Current holders do not reapply unless they qualify for a higher amount. Applications for the higher amounts go to the local assessor before April 1, 2027, and the figures are multiplied by the local certified ratio. Both statutes tie the exemption to a permanent resident who has owned the homestead for the preceding 12 months.

sections.h2: Selling a house with a homestead exemption
sections.html:
The exemption affects who owes what in the year of the sale, and it can change what a buyer pays the next year. Maine taxes what you own on April 1, and the tax year runs April 1 to March 31 under 36 M.R.S. §502.

Closing usually involves a proration. Under §558 a buyer and seller may split property tax pro rata over the municipality's fiscal year, unless they agree on a different period. Your bill already reflects your exemption for that year, so the proration uses the lower number.

A buyer does not inherit your exemption. A buyer who will live in the house files their own application by April 1, and the town applies it to the next assessment. A buyer who cannot meet the twelve-month ownership test, or who plans to rent the house out, may not get the same bill you did. Tell a buyer who is looking only at your old tax bill.

The state also charges a real estate transfer tax of $2.20 per $500 of value, split equally between buyer and seller under §4641-A.

sections.h2: Inheriting a house that had a homestead exemption
sections.html:
An inherited house that no one lives in will usually lose the exemption, because it rests on the owner using the home as a permanent residence. The break stays in effect only while ownership and residency are unchanged. Ask the assessor how the town handles a death.

Heirs who plan to sell should watch the April 1 date. If the owner died after April 1 and the exemption was in place that day, the town has already set that year's bill. If the house sits vacant into the next tax year, expect a full bill with no exemption. Our Maine probate guide explains who has authority to sell the property.

The State Property Tax Deferral Program matters most at closing. To qualify, you must be 65 or older or unable to work due to permanent disability, with household income under $80,000 and liquid assets under $100,000 ($150,000 with multiple owners). The state pays the tax, then places a lien on the home. Selling or transferring the home requires repayment of all deferred taxes, interest and costs. If a sale ends your time in the program, the payoff comes out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: Check your homestead status before listing
sections.html:
• Owners who moved out and are renting the house. The home is no longer the permanent residence, so the exemption may have ended.
  • Owners who bought a second Maine home in the last year. You can have only one permanent residence.
  • Heirs holding a vacant house. Ownership has changed and residence has stopped.
  • Owners with a deferral lien. Expect a payoff figure from Maine Revenue Services at closing.

If any of these fits and the house needs work you cannot afford before a sale, a direct sale to a cash buyer can simplify the tax side, since there is no buyer financing or inspection renegotiation holding up the proration. That is the kind of situation Cash Home Buyers works with, and we do not promise a price until we see the property.

faqs.q: Is the Maine homestead exemption still $25,000?
faqs.a: Yes. It is up to $25,000 of just value, multiplied by your town's certified ratio, and the base stays at $25,000 under the new section starting April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to apply, and do I reapply every year?
faqs.a: April 1, filed with your municipal assessor. A form filed after April 1 applies to the next year's assessment. You do not reapply each year, since the exemption stays in effect while ownership and residency do not change.

faqs.q: Does the buyer get my homestead exemption when I sell?
faqs.a: No. The exemption belongs to the permanent resident who owns and lives in the home. A buyer who will live there files their own application by April 1.

faqs.q: Can I get the exemption on a camp or second home?
faqs.a: No. Camps, vacation homes and second residences do not qualify, and you can have only one permanent residence at a time.
The old section 683 is discontinued for tax years beginning April 1, 2027, but section 683-A takes over with a base exemption of up to $25,000, plus veteran and blind exemptions.
